scene.testo: Sixteen sunrises. Sixteen sunsets. Every single day. That is what astronauts see from the International Space Station. Imagine you are floating inside it right now. No ceiling, no floor, no up. Your alarm just went off at 6 AM. Welcome to the strangest workday ever.

The station circles Earth about 250 miles up. It moves at 17,500 mph. That is roughly five miles every second. You cross the entire United States in about 10 minutes. And yes, you have a full job to do up here.

So here is the question. What do astronauts actually do all day? Not the movie version. The real schedule. Hour by hour. Stay with me, because the answer starts with the most awkward part of the morning: getting out of bed.

You do not sleep in a bed. You sleep in a sleeping bag fixed to a wall, inside a space about the size of a phone booth. Float or not, it feels the same. Your arms drift upward unless you tuck them in.

There is no morning light through a window. The station sees a sunrise about every 90 minutes, so crews follow Greenwich Mean Time instead. Most crews aim for about eight hours of sleep. Many report that it is hard to get.

Now you wake up. First problem: nothing stays put. Your toothbrush floats away. Your pillow is a bag. And without gravity pulling fluid down, your face looks puffy. Astronauts describe this as a permanent head cold feeling.
Washing is different too. There is no shower. You use rinseless soap and warm water from a pouch, with a towel. Water on the station does not fall. It clings to your skin in balls. You wipe it off.

Then comes the bathroom. The toilet uses airflow instead of gravity. You strap in with a bar across your thighs. Air pulls everything away. Urine is recycled into drinking water. Yes, really. NASA says the system recovers about 90 percent of the water.

Breakfast time. Your food comes in pouches and cans. Some of it you rehydrate with a needle that injects hot water. Crews have eaten tortillas instead of bread for years, because crumbs float and can clog equipment or drift into eyes.

Drinks come in sealed bags with a straw. Open a cup and the liquid floats out in a wobbling ball. Astronauts have even drunk coffee from special cups shaped so the liquid creeps up the side toward your mouth.

By about 8 AM, the work begins. A daily planning call connects you to mission control in Houston. They read the day's schedule. Every task is timed, usually in blocks of minutes. Your day is planned almost like a train timetable.

What is the work? Mostly science. The station carries labs where crews run experiments in biology, physics, and medicine. Some of them cannot be done on Earth, because gravity changes how flames burn, how crystals grow, and how cells behave.

Some days you are the lab rat. Crews take blood samples, measure their eyes, and scan their bones. Without gravity, bones can lose density. NASA studies show astronauts can lose about one percent of bone mass per month without countermeasures.

Other days you are a plumber, an electrician, a mechanic. The station is about the size of a football field from end zone to end zone. It never stops needing repairs. Filters, pumps, and fans all need care.

Let's measure it. The station's truss spans about 357 feet. A football field including end zones is 360 feet. So when you float from one end to the other, you are crossing something about as long as a football field.

Inside, the living space is roughly like a six-bedroom house. Sounds big. But it is full of racks, cables, and gear. Add noise from fans running around the clock, and it is closer to living in a very busy workshop.

Around noon, you break for lunch. Crews often eat together at the table in the Russian and US sections. Everyone clips in or floats near. Food is passed around and swapped. A favorite trade is spicy pouches for sweets.

Now the part nobody expects. You must exercise. Two hours every day. This is not optional. It is medicine. Without gravity, muscles and bones weaken fast. So the schedule treats the gym like a mandatory meeting.

You run on a treadmill held down by a harness with bungee cords. You lift weights on a machine that uses vacuum cylinders instead of metal plates. You ride a stationary bike. Sweat does not drip. It clings to you in beads.

Some days bring something bigger: a spacewalk. You put on a suit that weighs about 300 pounds on Earth. It has its own oxygen, water, and cooling. Preparing for it takes hours. Breathing pure oxygen first clears nitrogen from your blood.

Outside, temperatures swing wildly. In direct sunlight, surfaces can reach +250°F. In shadow, they can drop to -250°F. Your suit has to protect you from both. And every 90 minutes, you cross from one extreme to the other.
A typical spacewalk lasts about six to eight hours. You use tethers so you never drift away. Tools are tied to your suit too. Drop a wrench and it is gone forever, orbiting Earth on its own.

Below your boots, Earth rolls by. You can see oceans, storms, city lights. Astronauts often say the view changes how they think about home. Many describe the thin blue line of the atmosphere as shockingly fragile.

Back inside, there is cleanup. Cleaning is a daily job. Air filters collect dust and hair that float and gather. Surfaces get wiped down. In a closed home with no open windows, germs and mold are a real concern.

In the evening, you get some free time. Many crews spend it looking out the window. Cupola, the seven-window dome, is a favorite spot. You can watch lightning flash inside storms and the glow of cities at night.

You also call home. Crews have video calls with family and friends. They can even call the president, or schoolkids, through radio and video links. Time delays are tiny at this distance, so conversations feel almost normal.

Dinner is the social anchor of the day. People gather, swap stories, and share food. Crews have celebrated birthdays and holidays with special pouches. Sometimes, a fresh fruit delivery arrives, and it feels like a feast.
About 9:30 PM, the lights dim. You write notes, check the next day's plan, and climb into your bag. Over the next hour, the station crosses the night side of Earth, and you drift off.
Now compare that with your day. You wake up, shower, drive, sit at a desk, and walk the dog. Astronauts do a version of the same things. But every ordinary action takes extra thought and extra time.

A simple task like drinking water or moving a bag requires a plan. Without gravity, you push off a wall and glide. Misjudge it and you bump into a rack. Veterans say it takes a few weeks to feel natural.

Crews stay for about six months on typical long missions. Some stay close to a year. That is roughly 180 days of this routine, with a few days off, and every day built around work, exercise, and teamwork.

Then comes the return. The crew climbs into a capsule, undocks, and falls back through the atmosphere. Reentry heat is extreme. Parachutes open, and the capsule lands, either on land in Kazakhstan or splashing into the ocean.

And here is the most surprising detail. After months in space, your body has forgotten gravity. Astronauts often describe feeling heavy, dizzy, and clumsy. Even lifting a pen feels strange. Recovery takes weeks of rehab.

So what do astronauts do all day? They work, they exercise, they fix things, and they look out the window. It is both ordinary and extraordinary. And the next time you see the station pass overhead, remember someone up there is brushing their teeth.

descrizione:
What do astronauts actually do all day? In this documentary from Orbital Days, we follow a typical day aboard the International Space Station, from waking up in a sleeping bag at 6 AM to the final lights-out. Discover how astronauts eat, wash, exercise two hours a day, run science experiments, and go on spacewalks at 250 miles above Earth.

You will learn how crews use the toilet, why they eat tortillas instead of bread, how they stay healthy without gravity, and what temperatures from -250°F to +250°F mean for a spacewalk. All facts are based on NASA, ESA, and astronaut accounts.

If you love space, daily life on the ISS, and real NASA footage, subscribe to Orbital Days for more. Tell us in the comments what you would miss most on Earth.
